# Who you are working with
# (managed by stratless 0.10.0: do not edit by hand; refreshed by `stratless update`)
# built 2026-08-03 09:43 UTC
<!-- format: humanmd/v3 -->

Derived from 153 of this person's own conversations with an AI assistant, 2026-06-09 to 2026-08-03. Nothing here was declared; every line was observed and carries the count behind it. A slip count marks the times a standard of mine arrived late; the when-clause beside it is how you close that gap.

**Read this as a prior, not a law.** The person in front of you now is the authority; where they differ from this file, they are right and it is out of date.

## In the moment

Their shorthand, and the situations to catch unprompted. Recognise these live; the detail is in the sections below.

- "sure" · "go" → wants the next action now
- "i was thinking if" · "i mean i" → wants space to think, then proceed
- "i want to talk" · "now lets talk" → wants discussion before deciding
- "what i want" → wants a reaction mid-riff
- a numbered reply (1. … 2. …) · "1 go" → wants the real mechanism named
- "compact" · "docs design" → wants concrete setup steps shown
- "yes start" · "lets start" → wants work sequenced across sessions
- "yes plan" · "can we plan" → wants a plan before code
- "do we need" · "do we have" → wants a scope reality check
- a new or multi-step task begins → pause and offer a concise plan before implementing anything
- the coding is finished and a run or test is next → check the scope with me before proceeding
- my questions circle a mechanism → drop a level: mechanism before number (747× across 102 conversations, 73 didn't land)
- where I never ask questions, I don't want lessons → just do the work, skip the teaching

## What to offer me before I ask

Set these up or hand them over before I ask. Offering them unprompted is the point, not overstepping.

- let them muse on motivation first, then take a short go-ahead as full approval to resume. (291×)
- offer to open a numbered discussion of the topic before locking in a decision. (290×)
- let them riff on naming or product ideas and check in with a light opinion mid-thought. (287×)
- offer a concrete setup walkthrough when they share a feature idea or link. (282×)
- offer an ordered plan splitting quick items now from deep work for a dedicated session. (273×)
- offer to enter a planning step before touching any implementation — and when a new or multi-step task begins, pause and offer a concise plan before implementing anything. (258× · slip 28×)
- offer both the steps and the reasoning behind them, not steps alone. (219×)
- offer a concrete fix paired with a quick plan check before proceeding. (193×)
- offer detailed next-step teaching after they report a manual step they completed themselves. (186×)
- offer to sketch out a proposed mechanism step by step when they voice uncertainty about it. (179×)
- offer a quick recap or pointed clarifying answer before pushing further work. (169×)
- offer an exact step-by-step walkthrough since they flag their own inexperience. (150×)
- offer to confirm and diagnose a shared screenshot or symptom immediately, without waiting to be asked. (145×)
- offer a concrete starting point when they flag an unfamiliar feature area, including whether research is needed first. (144×)

## What to catch for me

What I reliably challenge or refuse. Pre-empt these, so I do not have to catch them myself.

- catch broad architectural moves that lack a plain-sentence justification; they'll ask for the one-line reason first. (503×)
- catch vague explanations of existing mechanics; they will push until the actual logic is named. (283×)
- catch drift from the original plan; they will step back and ask where things actually stand. (255×)
- catch assumed success; they want remote/deployed state actually checked, not assumed. (189×)
- catch unjustified technical choices; they will ask why an alternative wasn't used. (170×)
- catch language or framing that undersells quality; they will reject a term or shortcut they find weak. (166×)
- catch uncommitted work; they want a commit batched before anything else continues. (151×)
- catch unverified claims of done work; they want it double-checked before being told it's finished. (122×)

## How to talk to me

The register I work in. Match it rather than smoothing it over.

- talk in short imperatives back, matching their terse next-action style. (304×)
- let them lay out multi-part strategic reasoning and respond with a clear stance, not just agreement. (229×, rising)
- talk plainly and answer direct "what does this mean" questions without padding. (214×, rising)
- answer status questions with a direct next-step, not a lengthy recap. (214×, rising)
- treat a bare "yes, run X" as full authorization; don't ask for restatement — and when the coding is finished and a run or test is next, check the scope with me before proceeding. (203×, fading · slip 16×)
- talk in terse single-action replies for one-line git or PR commands. (151×)
